1023.title: St Patrick (17 March)
1023.hook: the breastplate prayer: Christ with me, Christ before me, Christ behind me
1023.howItsDone: Catholic and Anglican churches, and some others, keep St Patrick's feast with services and prayers, and the Breastplate is sung as a hymn or said as a morning prayer in some churches; in Ireland it is also a national holiday.

segments.voice: Yesterday, three forties: Moses, Elijah, Jesus, and each one with a far side. Your line was forty is enough. What did you choose to keep? Day one thousand twenty-three.

Green rivers, marching bands, plastic hats, a parade down the main street of cities that are nowhere near Ireland. That's one St Patrick's day. There's another, much quieter, and it starts with a short piece of writing by the man himself. In it he doesn't sound like a hero. He sounds embarrassed. He says he was not a learned man, that he writes clumsily, that as a young man he didn't really know God. And then he tells how he was stolen from his home, carried across the sea and made a slave in a strange country. The parade remembers a national saint. His own words remember a kidnapped boy. Today, St Patrick.
screen: `A SHORT ACCOUNT BY THE MAN HIMSELF.`

segments.voice: Patrick's own account is called his Confession, and it's worth hearing in outline. He grew up in Britain, in a Christian family, but he says he paid its faith little attention. Raiders took him captive to Ireland, where he was set to watch flocks on the hillsides. And there, alone, cold and hungry, he began to pray, he says, day and night, in snow and frost and rain. After years of this, a voice in his sleep told him a ship was ready. He ran, found the ship, and got home. That should be the end. Instead he dreams of a man bringing letters, and one of them is headed the voice of the Irish, calling him, as he tells it, to come and walk among them again. And he goes back. Back to the country of his slavery, to spend his life there. That's the man the prayer is pinned to. Tradition gives Patrick a hymn called the Breastplate, a prayer you put on like armor before going out. Whether he wrote it himself is uncertain; it isn't in his Confession. But it sounds like someone who knows what it is to be alone in a hostile place. Its familiar lines, in one English version, go: Christ with me, Christ before me, Christ behind me, Christ in me, Christ beneath me, Christ above me, Christ on my right, Christ on my left. Every direction is covered. Nowhere is left empty. Some readers hear in it the shepherd boy on the hillside, finding out he was never actually alone. The shamrock and the snakes come later, from legend. The Confession is where the man himself speaks.
screen: `THE VOICE OF THE IRISH CALLS HIM BACK.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: walk slowly through the directions of the breastplate. Sit or stand, and breathe. Notice what's in front of you. Then behind. Then the ground beneath you, the sky or ceiling above, your right side, your left. Take your time with each one. If you pray, you can say the lines as you go: Christ before me, Christ behind me, Christ beneath me, Christ above me, Christ beside me. If you don't, simply notice that you are held on every side, by the floor, the air, the room, the people somewhere near. Then rest in the middle of it. The bell holds the time.
St Patrick. A boy taken as a slave to Ireland who escaped, then chose to go back, and whose name is tied to a prayer that fills every direction with Christ.
Your line: christ beside me. Today, when you walk into a room that makes you nervous, notice who and what is beside you before you speak. Day one thousand twenty-three.

go back to the country of your slavery.
fork.reveal: he went back. by his own account, he spent his life in Ireland, the land where he had once been a slave.

trapdoor: what you thought: parades, green beer, and shamrocks.
what it means: a kidnapped boy who found God as a slave, escaped, and went back to the land of his captivity.
what a scholar hears: Patrick's Confession is his own account; the Breastplate is given to him by tradition, and its authorship is uncertain.

1024.title: St Joseph (19 March)
1024.hook: the quiet carpenter, patron of workers and fathers
1024.howItsDone: Catholics keep the solemnity of St Joseph in March, and in parts of Italy and among Italian-American families, St Joseph's tables of food are set out and shared with the poor; Anglicans and some Lutherans also keep his day.

segments.voice: Yesterday, St Patrick: a kidnapped boy who went back, and a prayer that fills every direction. Your line was christ beside me. Where did you notice it? Day one thousand twenty-four.

Go through the Gospels looking for a single sentence spoken by Joseph, the husband of Mary. You'll come up empty. He has dreams. He gets up in the night. He takes a pregnant fiancée into his home, walks a family to Egypt and back, searches the city for a missing twelve-year-old. And the text never once records him saying a word. Mary speaks. Simeon speaks. Angels speak. Joseph acts. Then, after the stories of Jesus's childhood, he never appears in a scene again. Churches still give him a feast day, and some honor him as the patron of workers and fathers. A whole saint's day for a man who never speaks. Today, St Joseph.
screen: `HE DREAMS. HE GETS UP. HE GOES.`

segments.voice: Matthew's story of Joseph opens at a painful moment. Mary, the woman he's promised to, is pregnant, and not by him. The King James Bible says: "Then Joseph her husband, being a just man, and not willing to make her a publick example, was minded to put her away privily." That comes first. Before any angel, his first instinct is to protect her from shame. He could have made it public, and he chooses to do it quietly. Then the angel comes in a dream and tells him not to be afraid to take Mary as his wife. And here is all Matthew gives us of his response: "Then Joseph being raised from sleep did as the angel of the Lord had bidden him, and took unto him his wife." No speech. No argument. He wakes up and does it. The pattern repeats. Another dream: take the child and flee. Matthew says he arose and took the young child and his mother by night, and departed into Egypt. Up in the dark, packing, gone. Later, when the danger is over, the same again, home. Then there's his work. In his home town, people later ask about Jesus, "Is not this the carpenter's son?" The Greek word behind carpenter means a builder or craftsman, someone who works with his hands. Mark's Gospel calls Jesus himself the carpenter, so tradition pictures him learning the trade from this quiet man. That's why Catholics in particular honor Joseph as patron of workers and of fathers, and of families. Some Orthodox and Protestant Christians honor him too, as the righteous man who sheltered the holy family. Across these traditions, the picture is of faith that shows up mostly as getting up and doing the next thing.
screen: `A JUST MAN, MINDED TO SPARE HER SHAME.`
`RAISED FROM SLEEP, HE DID AS BIDDEN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: think of a father figure in your life. Your own father, if that's a good place to go, or a grandfather, an uncle, a coach, a teacher, an older neighbor who once fixed your bike and asked nothing for it. Someone who mostly showed up rather than talked. Settle, and breathe. Let one specific thing they did come back to you, as clearly as you can. If you pray, you can thank God for them by name. If you don't, simply hold the memory with gratitude. Then decide how you'll thank them, or honor them if they're gone. The bell holds the time.
St Joseph. The husband of Mary and the carpenter of Nazareth, who in the Gospels never speaks, and keeps getting up to do what he was asked.
Your line: the quiet one. Today, send a short thank-you to someone who looked after you without fuss, and name the thing they did. Day one thousand twenty-four.

what it means: a just man who protected Mary, obeyed his dreams without a word, and is remembered as the carpenter who raised Jesus.
what a scholar hears: tektōn, a craftsman; and the Gospels record no words from Joseph at all — only what he did.

1025.title: The Annunciation (25 March)
1025.hook: nine months before Christmas; once the start of the new year in England
1025.howItsDone: Catholic, Orthodox and Anglican churches keep the Annunciation as a major feast in spring, and in some places the Angelus is still rung or prayed at morning, noon and evening.

segments.voice: Yesterday, St Joseph, who never says a word in the Gospels and keeps getting up to act. Your line was the quiet one. Who did you thank? Day one thousand twenty-five.

Count forward nine months from today and you land on Christmas. The feast of the angel's visit to Mary is kept in spring, a pregnancy's length before the birth. And for a long stretch of English history, this was also the day the year itself turned over. Not midwinter. Late March. Dates on letters and legal papers changed their year here, on the feast English people called Lady Day. A country turned its calendar on a conversation in Nazareth. Today, the Annunciation.

Luke opens the scene with a time stamp of his own: "And in the sixth month the angel Gabriel was sent from God unto a city of Galilee, named Nazareth." The sixth month of her cousin Elizabeth's pregnancy. So the story itself is already counting months. Gabriel comes in and greets her: "Hail, thou that art highly favoured, the Lord is with thee: blessed art thou among women." Luke says she was troubled, and wondered what kind of greeting this was. Then the message: she will conceive and bear a son, and call his name Jesus. She asks how, since she has no husband. The angel answers, and she gives her reply: "Behold the handmaid of the Lord; be it unto me according to thy word." Back in Advent we stayed with that yes. Today the feast asks something else of it: to notice when. Christian tradition holds that this is the moment God took flesh, not at the manger but here, hidden, months before anyone could see. Some readers see that thinking behind keeping the feast nine months before Christmas, and behind once starting the year here. The new thing had begun, even if it didn't show. For a long time, church bells marked the moment every day too. The Angelus, rung in some Catholic and Anglican places morning, noon and evening, is a short prayer that walks back through this scene: the angel's message, Mary's answer, and the Word made flesh. Tradition pictures farmers in the fields stopping at the bell. Noon in the middle of a working day, set aside to remember Mary's yes in a house in Nazareth.
screen: `BE IT UNTO ME ACCORDING TO THY WORD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: rehearse a noon pause. Right now, set a reminder on your phone for midday, or tie it to something that already happens around then, like lunch. Then settle, and breathe, and practice what you'll do when it comes. Stop your hands. Look up. Take three slow breaths. If you pray, you can say Mary's answer: be it unto me according to thy word. If you don't, simply ask yourself what you are saying yes to today, and let that be enough. Then sit in the quiet that follows. The bell holds the time.
The Annunciation. The angel's announcement to Mary, kept as a feast nine months before Christmas, the hidden start of the Christmas story.
Your line: nine months to go. Today, at noon, stop for one minute and name something that's begun in you but doesn't show yet. Day one thousand twenty-five.

1026.title: Mothering Sunday
1026.hook: in Britain and Ireland, mid-Lent: a day to visit the mother church and your mother
1026.howItsDone: In Britain and Ireland, Mothering Sunday falls in the middle of Lent; churches often give children flowers to hand to their mothers, and families send cards, visit or share a meal.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Annunciation, a feast kept nine months before Christmas. Your line was nine months to go. What has begun in you that doesn't show yet? Day one thousand twenty-six.

A young woman walks along a country lane early on a Sunday in spring, in her one good dress, with a bunch of wildflowers she picked from the hedge. She works as a servant in a big house miles away, and this is one of the few days of the year she's let go home. She'll go to the church where she was baptized, and then to her mother's door. That's the scene tradition paints of this day in Britain and Ireland, in the middle of Lent, when the fast eased for one Sunday and people went back to where they came from. Today it's mostly cards and flowers. Underneath, there's an older idea of who your mother is. Today, Mothering Sunday.

Start with the church calendar. In the middle of Lent's long weeks, the Western church kept a Sunday with a lighter tone. Its old opening words came from Isaiah, in the King James Bible: "Rejoice ye with Jerusalem, and be glad with her, all ye that love her." A day to rejoice, in the middle of the fast. And in the English prayer book, the letter read that Sunday came from Galatians, where Paul writes: "But Jerusalem which is above is free, which is the mother of us all." Jerusalem as a mother. The church as a mother. So the first mothering, tradition says, was going back to your mother church: the church where you were baptized, or the great church of your area. People who had moved away came home for it. Then, naturally, they went home to their actual mothers too. The custom grew warm edges. Servants were given the day. Children picked flowers on the walk. Some families baked a rich fruit cake, allowed in the eased fast. Over time, the church side faded for some families and the mother side stayed, and in Britain and Ireland, Mothering Sunday became the day for cards, flowers and phone calls home. Some confuse it with the American Mother's Day. It's a different day with a different history: one grew from a Sunday in the church year, the other began separately, in America. Set the two halves of the old custom side by side: a place that made you, and a person who made you. The old answer to both was the same: a walk down the lane, flowers from the hedge, and a knock at the door.

Here's the practice: walk the road home in your mind, the way the servant walked the lane. Settle, and breathe. Start from where you are. Take the route, street by street, to a door where someone mothered you: your own mother's, or a grandmother's, an aunt's, a neighbor's, a friend's mom who fed you. Whichever door you can walk up to gladly. Notice the step, the handle, the smell when it opens. Let one kindness from that house come back, a plate set down, a coat buttoned. If you pray, you can name her before God as you stand on the step. If you don't, simply stand there with her a moment. Then pick the hour today when you'll call her, or call someone who knew her. The bell holds the time.
Mothering Sunday. A Sunday in the middle of Lent when people in Britain and Ireland went back to their mother church, and then to their mothers.
Your line: go home. Today, call your mother or a mother figure, and tell her one thing you remember from her kitchen or her door. Day one thousand twenty-six.

what a scholar hears: the old readings — Isaiah 66:10 'rejoice ye with Jerusalem' and Galatians 4:26 'the mother of us all' — set the church as mother first.

1027.title: Lazarus Saturday
1027.hook: the Orthodox celebrate Lazarus raised, the day before Palm Sunday
1027.howItsDone: Orthodox Christians keep Lazarus Saturday the day before Palm Sunday, with a service that retells John 11 and, in some places, by making palm crosses or special breads for the next day.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mothering Sunday: a day to visit the mother church, and your mother. Your line was go home. Where did home turn out to be? Day one thousand twenty-seven.

A message reaches Jesus from two sisters in Bethany, Mary and Martha. In the King James Bible it's one line: "Lord, behold, he whom thou lovest is sick." Their brother Lazarus. And Jesus waits. He stays where he is two more days. By the time he reaches Bethany, Lazarus has been in the grave four days. Martha comes out to meet him on the road, and later Mary falls at his feet, and each of them says the same sentence: if you had been here, my brother would not have died. Then Jesus stands in front of a cave with a stone across it and asks for the stone to be rolled away. Martha, practical to the end, warns him about the smell. On the Saturday before Palm Sunday, Orthodox Christians tell this whole story again. Today, Lazarus Saturday.

John tells this one slowly, and three short lines carry it. The first is two words long: "Jesus wept." He stands with the sisters at the grave, and he weeps. John doesn't skip the grief to hurry on to the miracle, and neither does Jesus. The second line is a shout. In the King James: "Lazarus, come forth." And the dead man comes out, still bound hand and foot in grave clothes, his face wrapped in a cloth. The third line is easy to miss. Jesus turns to the people standing around and says: "Loose him, and let him go." Notice who does what. Jesus calls him out. Everyone else has to do the unwrapping. In this story, coming back takes a voice, and then a lot of ordinary hands working at knots. Now, why keep it on this particular Saturday? Because John sets the two scenes side by side. Right after Bethany, he says, a crowd that had heard about Lazarus took palm branches and went out to meet Jesus on the road into Jerusalem. So Orthodox churches treat this day as a hinge between Lent and Holy Week. They hear it as a preview of Easter: the one who calls his friend out of a tomb is about to walk toward his own. And John adds a hard detail. After the raising, the chief priests talk about putting Lazarus to death as well. Being called out of the grave didn't make his life safe. It made it visible.

Here's the practice: remember a friend who was restored. Someone who came back from something. An illness, a dark year, a long silence, a habit that nearly had them. Settle, and breathe. Bring their face to mind, the way it looked at the worst point, and the way it looks now. Then think about the hands. Who helped unwrap them? Maybe you were one of those hands. Maybe you only watched from a distance. If you pray, you can give thanks for them by name. If you don't, simply hold them in mind, glad they came out. The bell holds the time.
Lazarus Saturday. The day before Palm Sunday, when Orthodox Christians remember Jesus calling his friend out of the tomb at Bethany.
Your line: come out. Today, send one message to someone who's gone quiet for a long time, even if it only says their name. Day one thousand twenty-seven.

1028.title: Palm Sunday procession
1028.hook: crowds with palms, in some places olive or willow branches
1028.howItsDone: On Palm Sunday, congregations that keep the procession gather outside, have branches blessed, and process into church singing; in some churches the service then reads the Passion, the story of Jesus's arrest and death.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Lazarus Saturday: a voice at a tomb, and a crowd of hands to unwrap the man who walked out. Your line was come out. Whose name did you say? Day one thousand twenty-eight.

A coat lands in the dust of the road. Then another. Others are cutting branches from the trees and throwing them down. A man is coming down toward Jerusalem on a young donkey, and there are people ahead of him and people behind him, and all of them are shouting the same line. Mark says some spread their garments in the way and others cut branches off the trees. John says they were palm branches. On Palm Sunday, churches walk that road again. People gather outside, branches are blessed, and the whole congregation walks in together, carrying whatever grows near them: palms, and in some places olive or willow. Today, the Palm Sunday procession.

Start with the shout, because the crowd didn't make it up. Matthew gives it like this in the King James: "Hosanna to the son of David: Blessed is he that cometh in the name of the Lord; Hosanna in the highest." That middle line comes straight from Psalm 118, a song of thanks sung by someone arriving at the gates of the house of the Lord. The crowd reaches for words they already know by heart and hands them to the man on the donkey. Then the donkey. Matthew says this happened to fulfil a word of the prophet, and in the book of Zechariah it reads: "behold, thy King cometh unto thee: he is just, and having salvation; lowly, and riding upon an ass." A king, yes. But not on a war horse, and not with an army. Lowly. Some readers hear the whole scene as Jesus showing what kind of king he means to be. Now the branches. Only John names palms; Mark just says branches cut off the trees. The churches don't agree on one plant either. Where palms grow, people carry palms. Where they don't, people carry what's at hand, and in some places that's olive or willow. The point was never the species. It was a crowd laying something down in the road for someone they hoped in. And here's the turn that some churches keep on purpose. The same service that opens with branches and singing goes on to read the whole story of the arrest and the cross. The cheering and the crying out happen in one service, as they happened in one week. The road in leads to Friday.

Here's the practice: hold a branch or a leaf. A sprig from outside, a leaf from a houseplant, a stem from the kitchen. If there's nothing near, rest one hand open as if you were holding one. Settle, and breathe. Feel how light it is. A crowd laid things this small in the road for someone they hoped in. If you pray, you can say the crowd's line: blessed is he that cometh in the name of the Lord. If you don't, notice what you would lay down for someone you honor. The bell holds the time.
Palm Sunday procession. Churches walking in together with branches, the Sunday before Easter, retracing the crowd that welcomed Jesus into Jerusalem.
Your line: blessed is he who comes. Today, greet the next person who walks in, at your door, your desk, your table, as if their arriving were good news. Day one thousand twenty-eight.

1029.title: Holy Week's middle days
1029.hook: Monday to Wednesday: the fig tree, the temple, the anointing
1029.howItsDone: Some churches hold daily services on the Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday of Holy Week, reading the Gospel scenes of these days; some households use them to clean and prepare for Easter.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Palm Sunday procession: coats and branches on the road, and a crowd singing a psalm. Your line was blessed is he who comes. Who did you greet that way? Day one thousand twenty-nine.

So what happened on the Monday? Between the shouting on the road and the supper on Thursday, there are a few days that are easy to skip. Mark sets three strange scenes among them. A fig tree covered in leaves and bare of fruit. Tables tipped over in the temple courts, coins rolling on the stones. And a dinner in Bethany where a woman breaks open a jar of perfume and pours it over Jesus's head while the guests stare. Tradition spreads these scenes across the Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday of Holy Week. They feel like the held breath before everything happens. Today, Holy Week's middle days.

First, the tree. Jesus is hungry, sees a fig tree in leaf, and finds nothing on it. Mark even adds that it wasn't the season for figs. Jesus speaks to it, and the next morning it has withered from the roots. It's a hard little scene to read. Notice where Mark puts it: the tree comes before the temple scene and the withering comes after, so each frames the other. Some readers hear in it a warning about any religious life, their own included, that's all leaves and no fruit. Second, the temple. Jesus drives out the people buying and selling and overturns the money tables, and he quotes the prophets of Israel to do it. In the King James: "Is it not written, My house shall be called of all nations the house of prayer? but ye have made it a den of thieves." Of all nations. Some readers hear him defending the temple's own calling, in the words of its own scriptures. Third, the jar. At a dinner in Bethany, a woman breaks an alabaster jar of costly ointment over his head. Some at the table are indignant: what a waste. Jesus says, let her alone, and then: "She hath done what she could: she is come aforehand to anoint my body to the burying." He reads her gift as something the others hadn't seen yet: a burial anointing, ahead of time. Right after, Mark says, Judas goes to the chief priests. In some places Wednesday is called Spy Wednesday for that reason. Three scenes, and each one is quiet in its own way. A tree that says nothing. A courtyard cleared. A room full of perfume.
screen: `A HOUSE OF PRAYER FOR ALL NATIONS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: clean one room. For now, start with one corner of the room you're in. A shelf, a desk, the space by the bed. Pick up what's on the floor. Straighten what's crooked. Put one thing back where it lives. Go slowly, and breathe while you do it. The temple was cleared. The dinner room was filled with something costly. Either way, a space got ready for what was coming. If you pray, you can do this in silence as an offering. If you don't, just notice how the room changes when there's room in it. Holy Week's middle days. Monday to Wednesday before Easter, remembered through a fig tree, a cleared temple court, and a woman anointing Jesus at Bethany.

Your line: the quiet before. This week ran from Patrick's breastplate and Joseph's silence, through Mary's yes and going home, to an opened tomb and a road of branches. Today, do one small unseen job before the busy part begins. Day one thousand twenty-nine.
